policy.action: Suspend gold convertibility; monetize Treasury bills
policy.assessment: Classic wartime choice; prevents liquidity crisis; less painful than contraction

policy.action: Finance deficits with fixed 5% domestic war bonds, monetizing the shortfall
policy.assessment: Worked until 2H 1916; negative real rates then drove a self-reinforcing monetization spiral

policy.action: Borrow in foreign currency
policy.assessment: A bad sign; hard-currency debt cannot be printed away and exceeded gold reserves

policy.action: Allow depreciation rather than defend the mark with tight money; let inflation erode domestic debt
policy.assessment: Stimulative for exports, profits, employment, equities; real domestic debt cut to about 25%; classic have-nots-over-creditors choice

policy.action: Erzberger tax reform
policy.assessment: Raised direct-tax share to 75%; later a constraint since taxes already very high and reform watered down

policy.action: Deliberately depress the mark to restore competitiveness
policy.assessment: It worked: exports and employment recovered

policy.action: Easy Reichsbank policy (5% rate, bill purchases) and 10%-of-GDP deficits via floating debt
policy.assessment: Let Germany escape the 1920-21 global contraction but created dependence on hot money

policy.action: Respond to London Ultimatum by relying exclusively on money printing
policy.assessment: Policy makers wagered it was least terrible; Dalio: a mistake not to seek better balance between deflationary and inflationary levers

policy.action: Anchor market rates at 5% with inflation about 10x higher
policy.assessment: Produced borrowing/speculation surge and unproductive investment; reinforced the spiral

policy.action: Cannes compromise: 75% service cut for conditions incl. Reichsbank independence
policy.assessment: Mostly symbolic; taxes too small; independence used to print; still halted the slide for months

policy.action: Massive liquidity to banks via commercial bills and loan bureaus
policy.assessment: Prevented financial collapse but ten-fold money growth and shift in psychology to 'out of control'; printing was the least-bad option given French invasion threat

policy.action: Capital controls on FX purchases
policy.assessment: Classic lever, rarely successful; easy to evade and intensifies the urge to escape

policy.action: Dollar peg defended with borrowed FX; rate to 18%
policy.assessment: Worked three months then failed for lack of reserves; abandoned after six months; hyperinflation returned stronger

policy.action: Gold Loan bills indexed to dollars
policy.assessment: Disorganized and reactive; hoarded instead of circulating

policy.action: Restructure reparations (end passive resistance, Dawes committee, Dawes Plan)
policy.assessment: Critical precondition; without relief no new currency could have held; service cut to 1% of GNP

policy.action: Rentenmark then reichsmark with hard backing and credit caps
policy.assessment: An immediate 'miraculous' success because backing applied to all paper marks and the shrunken real money stock could be covered by reserves; endnote 140 says implicit gold backing mattered more than the mortgages

policy.action: End monetization of government debt; Rentenbank refuses the extra 400 million
policy.assessment: Signaled central-bank independence; necessary for confidence

policy.action: Close the deficit: index taxes, cut 25% of staff, cut salaries 30%, end Ruhr subsidies
policy.assessment: Extremely painful but tolerated after hyperinflation; stabilization itself raised real tax yields; surplus by January 1924

policy.action: Revalue private debts; cap private credit
policy.assessment: Tightened credit; painful short term but stabilized inflation (slightly negative May 1924)

policy.action: Rebuild FX reserves via repatriation and Dawes loan
policy.assessment: Ended the speculative attacks that threatened the stabilization

lessons.text: When money in circulation far exceeds gold backing and holders rush to convert, the central bank must tighten (defaults) or end convertibility and print; it nearly always prints because that is less painful.
Debt monetization is inflationary, lowers real rates, discourages lending to government, and so forces more monetization: a self-reinforcing spiral.
Hard-currency and gold-denominated debt cannot be printed away; foreign-currency borrowing is a bad sign.

Inflationary depressions are most common in countries without a reserve currency, with low FX reserves, large foreign debt, large and rising budget/current-account deficits, negative real rates, and a history of inflation and negative currency returns; Germany met all six by 1918.
Early in the cycle currency weakness causes the printing rather than the reverse: capital flight drives the currency down, which drives inflation.
Devaluations hurt importers and FX debtors but stimulate the economy and asset markets during weakness.
In crises, redistribution from haves to have-nots is more likely because the have-nots' conditions become intolerable and they outnumber the haves.
Deleveraging pain gives rise to populist and reactionary leaders on both left and right.
Many new buyers with no prior market experience is a classic bubble sign.
Capital inflows lower inflation and lift growth, outflows do the opposite; dependence on hot money leaves a recovery fragile and sentiment-driven.
A balance-of-payments crisis is like any payment problem: spend less, earn more, borrow or dissave, or default/get relief; a country additionally can change the amount and value of its currency.

Cases that become hyperinflations share one feature: policy makers never close the income/spending gap and keep funding it by printing; too much reflationary printing and devaluation relative to austerity and default produce the most severe inflationary depressions.
The inflationary spiral: impossible FX obligations -> currency decline -> inflation and liquidity crisis -> printing -> more capital flight.
A spending surge under rising inflation is flight from money, not real growth; real assets, durables, machines and stocks become inflation hedges.

In inflationary depressions each printing round sends more money out of the currency; at the hyperinflationary stage stopping is extremely hard because money is scarce even as it loses worth, and stopping would collapse the payment system.
Hyperinflations are not simply central banks recklessly printing; spirals push policy makers into printing as the least bad of terrible options.
As the spiral accelerates velocity rises; currency weakness leads inflation, which leads money growth.
Money loses its store-of-wealth role first, then its medium-of-exchange role.
Capital controls are a classic but rarely successful lever: easy to evade, and trapping people makes them want to escape more.

Ending hyperinflation requires restructuring the hard-currency debt, a hard-backed new currency, strict limits on printing and monetization, a closed deficit, tightened credit, and rebuilt FX reserves, applied comprehensively; none of it works unless the FX debt is actually reduced.

Currency credibility depends on the issuing institution; with few promises-to-deliver against it the central bank escapes the monetize-or-default dilemma, and limiting quantity to backing keeps it stable.
To build confidence in a new currency, monetization must stop; central banks should be independent of politics.
Once monetization stops the budget must be balanced, because new creditors are unavailable in an inflationary deleveraging.
Stabilization raises real tax receipts, creating a virtuous cycle.
Debt revaluations tighten credit, support the currency and lower inflation, the mirror image of debt reductions.
Without meaningful FX reserves, speculative attacks remain a threat even after sound reforms.

lessons.text: Debt growth is healthy when it finances activity that produces fast income growth.
Bubbles root in genuine productivity and technology gains plus leveraged bets that they continue.

Seven bubble marks: high prices vs traditional measures; prices discounting further rapid gains; broad bullish sentiment; purchases financed by high leverage; extended forward purchases; new buyers entering; stimulative policy inflating it and tightening popping it.
New, fast-growing lending channels outside regulated banking are symptomatic of bubbles; untested innovations lead to the next crisis.
Squeezing lenders and borrowers with asset/liability mismatches is a classic crisis ingredient.
Higher prices draw more supply and looser credit standards, the reverse of what logic suggests.
Banks look healthy in good times; trouble appears when deposits run and assets fall.
The worst debt bubbles come with asset inflation financed by debt rather than CPI inflation, so central banks targeting inflation accommodate too long.
Rising short rates flatten and invert the curve, raise the return on cash, pull money from assets and create a negative wealth effect; the bubble reverses into a bust.
No specific shock is needed to burst a bubble; unsustainable leverage-driven momentum and maxed positions suffice.
Normal-time checks and balances are poorly suited to crises requiring immediate aggressive action.
Sharp bear-market rallies classically recur during the depression phase.
Equities and credit-risk bonds fall while Treasuries and low-credit-risk assets rise in this phase.
Early in deleveragings, investors and policy makers underestimate real-economy weakness; rallies reverse and first responses are too small.
Widening spreads raise borrowing costs even as policy rates fall.
Protectionism and anti-immigrant sentiment classically rise in severe downturns.
Runs on non-guaranteed institutions are classic and can cause failure within days.
A gold standard is akin to foreign-currency debt; the toolkit is limited until the link is broken.
Banks are structurally vulnerable to runs through the liquidity mismatch; legal limits can block the lender of last resort.
Politics worsens depressions by blocking sensible policy or producing extreme policy.
Deficit worries and austerity are classic depression responses; since spending is income, cuts barely reduce debt/income ratios.
A widely lent reserve currency gets squeezed when credit creation in it collapses (dollar 1931 as in 2008).
Carry trades in good times set up worse bad times; wealth gaps feed populist extremists of both sides.
When systemically important institutions risk failing, policy makers must keep them running, especially in concentrated lender systems.
Big policy announcements repeatedly spark rallies within a 90% decline; moves that look small afterward feel huge at the time.
Making banks bear the cost is classic but misguided: politically necessary, financially disastrous.
Classic currency defenses (reserve sales, rate hikes, foreign loans) tend to fund the flight.
Devaluation and printing by an own-currency debtor start a beautiful deleveraging; bonds dip then rally.
In a balance-of-payments crisis, rate rises big enough to compensate currency risk are intolerable domestically and fail.
Rallies on liquidity programs fade when total money and credit do not change.
Policy makers play with deflationary levers for a couple of years before accepting that debt reduction and austerity are too painful and inadequate, then act aggressively.
Lending against widening collateral to wider borrowers is a classic liquidity lever for central banks or governments.
Abandoning mark-to-market is a classic bank-support move.
Main Street versus Wall Street outrage over bailouts makes needed rescues politically hard.
Austerity to balance the budget in a depression is a rookie move.
Expedient political promises inconsistent with fundamentals should never be believed.
Reliance on deflationary levers yields an ugly deleveraging: nominal rates above nominal growth so debt/income rises despite defaults.
Failing to rescue systemically important institutions spreads ripples through the whole system.
Capital controls are a classic but ineffective balance-of-payments response.
Providing liquidity rather than withholding it cures liquidity-driven runs; guarantee the banks kept open; support systemic banks, let small ones fail.
Breaking the gold link is required to print; the currency then falls against others and gold (1933 as in 1971), which is why timeless principles from history matter.
Leaving gold was the turning point; averages mask an uneven recovery that favored the rich.
Changing laws to prevent the last crisis is typical at the end of big debt crises.
A beautiful deleveraging needs enough stimulation to offset deflation and lift nominal growth above nominal rates.
The first tightening typically does not hurt stocks or the economy.
Competitive devaluations leave currencies roughly unchanged against each other, all devalued against gold.
Fear of repeating the 1920s bubble drove tightening into a fragile recovery; combined monetary and fiscal tightening caused the 1937 sell-off and recession.
Uneven recoveries that favor elites breed redistribution pressure and strikes.
Economic rivalry between rising and incumbent powers precedes military conflict; the 1930s wars effectively began about ten years before 1939/1941.
